chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
When a man slanders his wife, he does not perform li'an with her unless he says, 'I saw a man between her legs committing adultery with her.'

He (peace be upon him) was asked about the man who slanders his wife. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He performs li'an with her, then they are separated, and she is not permissible for him ever. If he confesses against himself before the li'an, he is whipped with the hadd penalty, and she remains his wife.'

And I asked him (peace be upon him) about the free woman whose husband accuses her, and he is a slave. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He performs li'an with her, then they are separated, and she is not permissible for him ever. If he confesses against himself after the li'an, he is whipped with the hadd penalty, and she remains his wife.'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'And I asked him about the free man who has a slave girl, and he accuses her. He (peace be upon him) said: 'He performs li'an with her.'

And I asked him about the woman subjected to li'an by her husband, who denies her child, and he performs li'an with her and separates from her. Then he says afterwards, 'The child is my child,' while lying about himself. He (peace be upon him) said: 'As for the woman, she does not return to him ever. As for the child, I return it to him when he claims it, but I do not consider it his child. There is no inheritance for him (the father in the child), and the son inherits from the father, but the father does not inherit the son, and its inheritance goes to its maternal uncles. If its father does not claim it, then its maternal uncles inherit it, and it does not inherit them. If anyone calls him the son of adultery, he is whipped with the hadd penalty.'
ai.seo_question: What are the Shia jurisprudential rules for li'an and the resulting lineage and inheritance of the child?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the precise mechanics of li'an (mutual cursing) as a procedural oath to establish paternity denial, emphasizing that the husband must specify seeing the act between the wife's legs for the curse to be valid. It further clarifies the permanent irrevocability of the separation (la tazuj) and the nuanced inheritance rights of the child, who retains lineage to the mother's family (akhwal) if the father denies him, reflecting the Shia juristic distinction between lineage (nasab) and inheritance (mirath).
